posts.character: Cars and driving culture (directions by landmark)
posts.quote: MOM GAVE DIRECTIONS BY LANDMARK, AND TURN WHERE THE WHITE BARN USED TO BE WAS A COMPLETE SENTENCE.
posts.caption: Mom never once said a street name. Her directions came in landmarks: turn at the big oak, pass the stand where we bought corn, and bear left where the Hendersons' barn used to be. That barn had been gone for six years, and nobody ever corrected her. Dad drove, we kids watched the road unroll out the back window, and somehow we always arrived. A stranger following those directions would have ended up in a cornfield, but we never once got lost.
posts.first: My mother's directions to her sister's house included a dead tree that fell before I was born. She said it with total confidence every time. We found the house on the first try, every time, and I still can't tell you how.

posts.quote: THE DRIVE-UP BANK SENT YOUR DEPOSIT THROUGH A TUBE, AND THE KIDS IN THE BACK SEAT WAITED FOR THE LOLLIPOP.
posts.caption: The bank had a drive-up lane with a clear tube that sucked your deposit away with a whoosh. You put the slip and the check in a plastic canister, pressed the button, and watched it disappear into the building. A minute later it came back with a stamped receipt and, if you were lucky, a lollipop rattling around inside. The kids in the back seat always knew about the lollipop before the grown-ups did. Nobody said a word about the cars lined up behind you, because everyone was waiting on the same whoosh.
posts.first: My dad let me push the button once, and I was sure I had sent the money to the moon. When it came back with a red lollipop, I decided banks were the best place in town.

posts.quote: THE TOWN DUMP WAS A SATURDAY OUTING, AND DAD ALWAYS CAME HOME WITH MORE THAN HE TOOK.
posts.caption: Saturday morning meant loading the trunk with the week's trash and driving out to the town dump. It was an outing, complete with a man in a booth who waved Dad through and gulls wheeling over everything. Dad would toss the bags, then wander off to look at what other people had thrown away. He came back once with a perfectly good floor lamp and once with a chair that only needed one leg. Mom would look at the lamp in the back seat and just sigh, and the lamp ended up in the living room anyway.
posts.first: Our rocking chair came from the dump in 1967. Dad glued the leg himself, and it outlasted the house. I still have it in my spare room.

posts.character: Childhood rituals (the bike on the porch)
posts.quote: Nobody owned a bike lock. You leaned the bike on the porch rail, and it was there in the morning.
posts.first: My first bike spent every night against the porch rail for six years, rain or shine. The only thing that ever happened to it was the seat getting a little more cracked.

posts.character: Old jobs and skills (the encyclopedia salesman)
posts.quote: THE ENCYCLOPEDIA MAN / A BRIEFCASE, A POLITE SPEECH, AND TWENTY-SIX VOLUMES PAID OFF BY THE MONTH
posts.caption: He came to the door in a pressed suit with a briefcase and a very good smile. Mom let him into the front room, and he opened the briefcase on the coffee table like he was unpacking treasure. There were sample pages with color maps, pictures of animals, and a shelf in the brochure that looked a lot like ours. He talked for an hour, and every child in the house sat at attention. By the end of the month, twenty-six volumes were lined up on the shelf, and you could look up anything except the cost.
posts.first: We got our set in 1964 on the monthly plan. I read the entry on volcanoes so many times the page came loose. Dad said it was the best money he ever spent on payments.

posts.character: Old jobs and skills (the knife sharpener)
posts.quote: THE KNIFE SHARPENER CAME DOWN THE STREET RINGING A BELL, AND EVERY MOTHER HAD A DRAWER READY.
posts.caption: You heard the bell before you saw him, a bright little ring at the end of the block. The knife sharpener pushed a cart with a grinding wheel, and he stopped in front of whichever house waved first. Mothers came out with butcher knives and kitchen scissors wrapped in dish towels. He worked the pedal, the wheel hummed, and a stream of sparks danced off the blade. The neighborhood kids stood in a ring, close enough to feel the heat and far enough to stay out of trouble.
posts.first: Our sharpener came on Thursdays, and Mom saved her good scissors for him. She said nobody else ever put a real edge on them. I can still hear that grinding wheel from across the street.

posts.quote: THE DIME STORE FLOOR CREAKED IN EVERY AISLE, SO THE CLERK ALWAYS KNEW WHERE THE KIDS WERE.
posts.caption: The dime store had wooden floorboards that complained under every step. Row after row of bins held ribbon, thimbles, rubber balls, and tin whistles, and the candy counter sat low enough for a child to see everything. You tried to tiptoe past the toy aisle, but the boards gave you away. From somewhere near the cash register a voice would say, I hear you back there. You put the little plastic horse back where you found it and walked out with a stick of gum.
posts.first: I spent my allowance there every Saturday. A nickel got me a paper bag of jelly beans if I stood at the counter long enough to decide. The clerk never rushed me.

posts.quote: GRANDMA WASHED THE ALUMINUM FOIL AND HUNG IT TO DRY, AND IT OUTLASTED HER REFRIGERATOR.
posts.caption: Grandma never threw away a sheet of aluminum foil in her life. After every meal she smoothed it flat on the counter, rinsed it in the sink, and pinned it to a string over the window to dry. By Sunday there was a row of silver sheets flapping gently above the sink like a tiny parade. She folded them into a drawer, and they came out again for the next pot roast. When her refrigerator finally gave out, the foil was still going strong, and she considered that a fair trade.
posts.first: I helped her pin the sheets up more times than I can count. She called it good housekeeping, and I called it a silver clothesline. We were both right.

posts.quote: THE POWER OUTAGE / TWO CANDLES, A DECK OF CARDS, AND THE WHOLE FAMILY AT ONE TABLE
posts.caption: The lights went out in the middle of supper, and the whole house went quiet for a second. Then somebody found the candles in the drawer by the stove, and the dining table glowed gold. Dad dug out a deck of cards, and nobody argued about whose turn it was. The storm rattled the windows, the radio sat silent, and for once the house felt like one room. When the lights came back on at ten, everybody groaned a little before reaching for the switch.
posts.first: We lost power every winter, and every winter Dad dealt the cards the same way. Mom always won at rummy and pretended she hadn't. I'd give a lot for one more of those nights.

posts.character: Values and community (shoveling the neighbor's walk)
posts.quote: DAD SHOVELED THE NEIGHBOR'S WALK BEFORE OUR OWN, AND NEVER ONCE MENTIONED IT.
posts.caption: After a heavy snow, Dad was out before sunrise with the metal shovel and a thermos of coffee. He started at Mrs. Kessler's house, because her husband had passed and her steps were steep. Then he did the Millers' walk next door, and only after that did he clear ours. He never knocked on a door or waited for a thank-you. By the time the sun came up, the whole block had a clear path, and nobody could say who had done it. We kids knew, and we kept quiet about it too.
posts.first: I went out with him one morning when I was nine and carried the thermos. Mrs. Kessler's porch light came on, and he lifted two fingers to the window without looking up. That was the whole conversation.
